c1.story:
Mining is the oldest business on this page and, in India, one of the most political. The ground belongs to the state. The biggest miner, Coal India, is owned by the state. The price of its main product is notified by the state. And yet sitting in the same sector are companies whose prices are set by traders on the London Metal Exchange, a world away from Delhi.

That is why mining in India is really four different businesses sharing a hard hat.

Door one is coal. Coal India, Bharat Coking Coal and GMDC dig it, and most of it goes to power plants under long fuel-supply agreements at prices the government notifies. The rest is sold through e-auctions, where buyers bid, and when coal is scarce those auctions clear at fat premiums. Coal India listed in 2010 in what was then India's largest IPO, and it has behaved ever since like a giant utility with a dividend habit.

Door two is the integrated metal major: Hindustan Zinc, Vedanta, NALCO and Hindalco. They own the mine and the smelter, and often the coal-fired power plant that feeds it. Hindustan Zinc's Rampura Agucha mine in Rajasthan is one of the largest zinc mines in the world; NALCO digs bauxite at Damanjodi in Odisha and smelts it at Angul. They sell metal at London prices while paying Indian costs, which puts them near the bottom of the world cost curve.

Door three is iron ore and bulk minerals: NMDC, Sandur Manganese, KIOCL, selling rock to steel mills at monthly posted prices. Door four is the processors and smaller miners: IMFA's ferrochrome, Graphite India's electrodes, Hindustan Copper, Sarda. They usually live off one product, and that product's price is often set in China.

The same copper rally can be a jackpot for one door, a footnote for another and a cost increase for a third.
c1.read:
Four tiles, one per door. Read each top to bottom, then compare the profit bars across the row.

  • The line under the name is how the product is priced. Coal: notified prices plus auction premiums. Metal majors: London prices. Iron ore: monthly posted prices tracking China. Processors: one product's market price, often Chinese.
  • The tickers open each company's page. A few names deserve a mental footnote: VEDL is a holding company with stakes in Hindustan Zinc and others, so its tile overlaps with HINDZINC's, and HINDALCO is as much a global aluminium-rolling business, through Novelis, as a miner.
  • The profit bar is the story of this card. Two doors show high: coal and the metal majors. That is unusual for a commodity sector, and it comes from owning the deposit. A coal miner with a near-monopoly and a metal major with captive ore and power keep most of what they earn. Iron ore sits at medium, since steel mills are powerful buyers and the government has taxed ore exports before. Processors sit at low, because they buy someone else's ore or power and sell into a Chinese-set price.
  • The bet line is what you are buying: power demand and a dividend, world metal prices against a low cost base, Indian steel output, or one product's price.

A quick test for any mining stock you own: does it own the rock, own the power, and set its own price? Three yeses is rare. Two is the metal majors. One or none is a processor.

c2.story:
Every mining kitchen starts with something you cannot manufacture: a deposit. In India the deposit belongs to the state, so station one is a government office. The Geological Survey of India maps what lies underground, the states auction the leases, and the winner promises a share of revenue for decades. Coal India and NMDC sit on legacy leases granted long ago, which is part of why they are so cheap to operate.

Station two is mining itself. Most Indian coal comes out of vast open-cast pits in Jharkhand, Odisha and Chhattisgarh, where giant shovels and dumpers do the work; zinc in Rajasthan comes from deep underground mines. Station three is beneficiation: crushing, washing and concentrating raw rock to raise its grade, because nobody wants to pay freight on dirt. KIOCL turns ore into pellets at Mangaluru; the coal companies run washeries.

Station four is the expensive part: smelting and refining. Turning alumina into aluminium needs staggering amounts of electricity, which is why Indian smelters sit next to their own coal-fired power plants. This is also where China looms largest. China smelts most of the world's aluminium, zinc and copper and refines most of its critical minerals. It is the world's biggest buyer and its biggest producer at the same time.

Station five is the buyer: NTPC and the state power utilities for coal, the steel mills for ore, galvanisers, cable makers and global traders for metal.

The most important thing about this kitchen is geography. Coal, ore and bauxite sit in the same eastern and central belt, so a smelter in Odisha can burn coal from the next district to make power to melt bauxite from the next hill. That co-location is the Indian miner's cost edge, and the reason the majors sit so low on the world cost curve.
c2.read:
Read the diagram in two passes: the five station boxes left to right, then the two band rows under them.

The boxes run from lease to buyer. Notice who stands where. Station one is the Ministry of Mines, the Geological Survey and the states, with Coal India and NMDC holding legacy leases. Station two is a crowded roster of listed miners. Station three is often the same miners doing their own washing, with KIOCL's pellets. Station four is the smelters, and its box names China outright.

The first band row labels who holds each station. Station one reads state auctions: the industry's starting point is a government decision. Stations two and three read India listed. Station four reads India listed and China together, the only station where the two share a cell. Station five is utilities and mills.

The second band row puts China across the producing stations and World under the buyers. For mining that row has two meanings, as the explainer's rival label says: China is a rival smelter and also the buyer whose demand sets the price. Few industries have their main competitor and their main price-setter be the same country.

The note below the diagram adds the geography: coal, ore and bauxite in the east and centre, zinc in Rajasthan, and smelters that follow the ore and cheap captive power. Use the diagram to trace news. A lease auction or a forest clearance is station one, and slow. A rake shortage hits stations two and five. A Chinese smelter curtailment hits station four, and lifts prices for every Indian smelter that is still running.

c3.story:
Here is a sentence that explains most of Indian mining: coal follows Indian electricity, and metals follow the world.

Start with coal. The single largest customer by far is the power sector, NTPC and the state electricity boards, which burn coal to keep the lights and air-conditioners on. When a heatwave pushes power demand to records, as it did in the spring of 2022, utilities scramble for coal, imported coal becomes eye-wateringly expensive, and Coal India's e-auction premiums explode. When the monsoon is generous, hydro dams run full, solar parks hum, and stockpiles at power plants pile up. Then the premium shrinks and Coal India becomes a steady, unexciting supplier. Cement plants, aluminium smelters and other industries buy the rest through those e-auctions, comparing the price with imported coal.

Metals are a different world. Zinc goes into galvanising steel, so it follows infrastructure and construction. Aluminium and copper go into power lines and cables, so they follow grid build-out, renewables and, increasingly, data centres, which are hungry for both power and the copper that carries it. Aluminium also goes into cars and drinks cans. Silver, which Hindustan Zinc recovers as a by-product of smelting zinc and lead, goes into solar panels, electronics and jewellery.

And above all of these sits China, which consumes about half the world's metals. A Chinese stimulus package lifts London prices; a Chinese property slump drags them down. Indian demand for metals is growing nicely, but it is not yet big enough to set the price.

A heatwave in Delhi helps Coal India. A slump in Shanghai hurts Hindustan Zinc. Both can happen in the same quarter.
c3.read:
Each tile is a customer group: who buys, what they buy, and what moves them. The useful trick is to sort the tiles into two piles.

  • The coal pile: power utilities, which take the bulk of Coal India's output and move with electricity demand, heatwaves, hydro and solar output; and cement, aluminium and other industries, which buy non-power coal in e-auctions and watch the imported coal price.
  • The metals pile: steel mills for iron ore and ferro alloys; construction and galvanising for zinc; transmission and cables for aluminium and copper; autos and packaging for aluminium sheet and cans; solar, electronics and jewellery for silver and copper; and export markets, which pay London prices.

Now read the third line of each tile in the metals pile. Several of them mention the energy transition: renewables, data centres, electric vehicles, solar installations. That is the structural story behind today's metals boom, and it is why copper, silver and aluminium have outrun zinc and iron ore.

The steel mills tile links this card to the steel industry's own explainer. NMDC's fortunes are a derivative of Indian steel output, and the Chinese steel exports in its third line are the same ones that cap Indian steel prices.

Finally, map your holdings. Coal India lives almost entirely on the first tile. Hindustan Zinc spreads across galvanising and silver. Hindalco and NALCO lean on cables, autos and exports. A miner on one tile is a bet on one customer's cycle.

c4.story:
A mine is a strange economic animal. Almost all its costs are fixed. The pit has to be dug, the dumpers have to run, the miners have to be paid and the smelter has to be kept hot whether the price of zinc is high or low. So when prices rise, almost all of the increase falls straight to profit. When prices fall, almost all of the fall comes out of profit too. Economists call this operating leverage; miners call it a good year or a bad year.

That is why the two numbers that matter most are realisation per tonne and cost per tonne. Realisation, for a metal major, is the London price plus a regional premium, converted to rupees. For coal, it is the notified price on fuel-supply contracts plus whatever the e-auctions fetched. Cost per tonne is where the company sits on the world cost curve, a chart that lines up every mine and smelter on earth from cheapest to dearest. The cheapest producers make money at almost any price; the dearest shut down when prices fall. Indian majors, with rich ore and captive coal power, sit near the cheap end.

The two doors spend differently. Coal India is a people business. It is one of the country's largest employers, and its biggest single cost is wages and pensions. Every few years a national wage agreement is signed, and the arrears can dent a year's profit. Smelters are a power business: electricity is the main cost of making aluminium and zinc, which is why owning a coal-fired captive plant, and increasingly renewables, is the edge.

In mining, management controls the cost line. The market controls everything else.

And then there is debt, which is mostly a non-issue for the state-owned miners and the defining issue for the Vedanta group, where the parent's borrowings pull cash up from listed subsidiaries through dividends and brand fees.
c4.read:
Two charts walk one hundred rupees of sales down to what is left: coal miners on one side, integrated base-metal majors on the other. Read each left to right.

  • The input bar here is not raw material in the usual sense, because a miner digs its own. It is royalty to the state, power and contractors. For coal miners it takes roughly three rupees in ten; for metal majors, a little more, because power for smelting is part of it.
  • The opex bar is people, freight and stores, and this is where the two doors split. For coal it is the biggest bite of all, close to four rupees in ten, because Coal India's wage and pension bill is enormous. For metal majors it is barely more than a tenth.
  • The depreciation and interest bar is small for both, a little bigger for the metal majors, whose smelters are costlier assets and where group debt adds interest.
  • The last bar is what is left. Both shapes keep a lot, which matches the high profit bars on card one, but the metal majors keep noticeably more, over four rupees in ten against under three for coal.

These are illustrative mid-cycle shapes, not any company's accounts. Hover a bar for the amount.

Below, the line list marks what to watch. Realisation, cost of production, employee cost and power cost all get a yes: two of them are the whole story for coal, the other two for smelters. Depreciation, capex, working capital and interest are sometimes. Interest in particular is a no-show for the state miners and a headline at Vedanta.

c5.story:
Most industries on this page are trying to climb out of a bust. Mining is the exception: the clock says boom, and it has already been round once since the pandemic.

The first boom came in 2021 and 2022. Stimulus money, tangled supply chains and then Russia's invasion of Ukraine sent metals and coal to records. Europe's energy crisis made electricity so expensive that aluminium and zinc smelters across the continent shut down, removing supply just as demand peaked. In India, a power crisis in the spring of 2022 left plants short of coal; the government pushed utilities to import and blend foreign coal, and Coal India's e-auction premiums went through the roof. Miners paid huge dividends.

Then 2023 brought the hangover. China slowed, metal prices fell, and with plenty of coal at the pitheads, e-auction premiums collapsed. Profits came off their peak, though for low-cost producers off the peak still meant very profitable.

By 2024 the bottom was in, and a new story was taking shape. Copper mines are hard to find, slow to build and declining in grade, while the world wants more copper for power grids, electric vehicles and data centres. Silver, needed for solar panels, tightened too. Aluminium recovered as Beijing kept its cap on its own smelting capacity.

So in 2026 the clock reads metals boom: copper, silver and aluminium near records. But the boom is lopsided. Coal is the laggard. India crossed a billion tonnes of coal output, power plants are sitting on full stockpiles, and premiums are thin. Coal India is having a perfectly decent, perfectly boring time while its metal cousins party.

In a boom, the question is never whether earnings are good. It is how long they stay good, and how much of that the share price already assumes.
c5.read:
Three pieces: the clock, the timeline and the four hands.

The clock has four arcs clockwise from the top: boom, peak, bust and bottom. The years under each arc are from the last cycle, which ran fast: boom in 2021 and 2022, peak in 2022, bust in 2023, bottom in 2024. The arrow points to today, and for mining it sits squarely in the middle of the boom arc, around half past one. Hover any arc for what defined that phase.

The timeline tells the story year by year, colour-coded by tone: a neutral 2019, the pandemic bust of 2020, the boom, the bust of 2023, a neutral stretch as copper and silver climbed, and the latest entry marked now. That last entry is worth reading twice, because it holds both halves of today: metals near records, coal the laggard.

The four hands are what to watch to move the arrow.

  • London aluminium, zinc and copper prices: near highs, arrow up. They lift the base-metal majors almost one for one.
  • Silver price: very strong, arrow up. A big swing factor for Hindustan Zinc.
  • Coal e-auction premium: thin, arrow down. Coal is plentiful.
  • Chinese industrial demand: soft with stimulus talk, a diamond. This is the hand that decides how long the boom lasts.

Three hands are about prices and they point up; the one about China is mixed. In a boom, watch the mixed hand most closely.

c6.story:
Who decides how much money Hindustan Zinc makes this quarter? Not Hindustan Zinc. Mostly it is a trader on the London Metal Exchange, a Chinese credit officer deciding whether to lend to property developers, a currency dealer in Mumbai and, for silver, a solar-panel buyer somewhere in the world.

Three dials carry the most weight. The aluminium price is the biggest single lever for Hindalco, NALCO and Vedanta, and because their costs barely move, a rise in aluminium lifts profits almost one for one. Indian electricity demand is the equivalent for Coal India: more power demand means more offtake and higher auction premiums. And Chinese demand and stimulus sits behind every London price, since China buys about half the world's metals.

Then come the two-dot dials. Copper and silver are rising stars, the energy-transition metals. The dollar matters in a friendly way here: Indian metal majors sell at dollar prices and pay costs in rupees, so a weaker rupee raises their realisations without raising their costs. Iron ore output and steel demand drive NMDC.

One dial is genuinely two-faced: domestic coal output. More output is good for Coal India's volumes but, if it outruns demand, it fills power-plant stockpiles and crushes the e-auction premium. That is exactly what has happened lately: record output, full stockpiles, thin premiums.

And one dial points the wrong way: government stake sales. When the government sells a slice of Coal India, NMDC or Hindustan Zinc through an offer for sale, it adds a wave of supply to the market, usually at a discount, and the share price tends to stall around it. It does not change the business at all, but it can change your returns for a few months.
c6.read:
Each row is one dial. Read across: the dial, the channel, what a rise does, and the weight.

  • Arrows: almost every row is green, which is typical of a sector whose profits rise with prices. Aluminium, copper, silver, power demand, the dollar, Chinese demand, iron ore and mining output all help when they rise. The diamond on domestic coal output marks the volume-versus-premium trade-off. The lone red arrow is government stake sales.
  • Weight: three dots on aluminium, Indian electricity demand and Chinese demand. Two dots on copper, silver, coal output, the rupee and iron ore. One dot on the monthly mining output index and stake sales.
  • Channel tells you which company feels each dial. It is the best column to use as a lookup: aluminium names Hindalco, NALCO and Vedanta; silver names Hindustan Zinc; electricity names Coal India.

The latest column is richer here than in most industries, because metal prices are series we track directly: aluminium, copper and silver show live readings, as do the core-sector electricity, coal and iron ore indices, the mining production index and the rupee. Chinese demand uses the Nifty Metal index as a proxy, which is a reasonable sense check since that index moves with the global metal mood. Stake sales show a dash; they come as news.

Use the table in pairs, as the so-what line suggests. Aluminium and power demand together tell you how the two halves of the sector are doing. If one is green and the other flat, as now, the sector's average hides a split.

c7.story:
India sits on some of the world's largest reserves of coal, iron ore and bauxite. So why does it still import coal, and why isn't it a mining superpower? The bottlenecks answer that question.

The first is the hardest: leases and land. Every new mine needs an auctioned lease, a forest clearance, an environmental clearance and land from villages whose families may have lived there for generations. Each step can take years, and any one can stall a project. The memory of the coal block allocation scandal, which ended in 2014 with the Supreme Court cancelling almost every block allocated since the early nineties, still shapes how cautious the system is. Since then the auction route has become the norm, which is cleaner but slower.

The second is China. It smelts most of the world's aluminium, zinc and copper and dominates the processing of critical minerals like rare earths, graphite and lithium. When Beijing tightens or loosens its own production, prices for everyone move.

Then the quieter ones. Coal's long decline is real: solar is growing fast, and while coal still runs most of India's power, a slow structural drift away from it is underway. Rail is the lifeline of mining, since coal and ore move by rake, and rake shortages in peak season strand output at the pithead. The Vedanta group's parent debt is a perennial overhang for its listed companies. Coal India's wage settlements arrive every few years as a lump of cost. And the monsoon floods open-cast mines every September quarter, so a weak July-to-September quarter is often the weather, not the business.

Finally, the state's own appetite. Royalties, district mineral fund levies and, since the Supreme Court's 2024 ruling, state taxes on mineral rights all tend to grow when prices rise. The state is a silent partner who asks for more in good years.
c7.read:
Each row is one bottleneck, with why it bites and a severity label. Mining's list has an unusual shape: half its rows are recurring.

  • Structural: leases and land, and Chinese dominance. These cap the sector permanently. Leases cap growth: new capacity always arrives later than planned. China caps pricing power: the world price is set elsewhere.
  • Slow: the coal transition. A decades-long drift, not a quarterly risk, but it is why the market pays a low multiple for Coal India despite its profits.
  • Recurring: rail logistics, Vedanta group debt, wage settlements and the monsoon. These are the predictable irritants. The monsoon row in particular is a calendar effect: expect weaker volumes in the September quarter every year, and do not mistake it for a trend.
  • Two-sided: the state's take. Higher royalties and taxes in a boom cap the upside, but the same arrangement makes the state an interested partner in keeping mines running.

Read the table in two halves. The first two rows explain why Indian mining earns a good but not spectacular share of global booms. The recurring rows are the ones that explain a single surprising quarter. When a mining result disappoints, check the recurring rows before rethinking the thesis.

The so-what line sums it up: China and the London price set the cycle, but leases, rail and the state's cut decide how much an Indian miner actually banks.

c8.story:
In most industries the regulator is a referee. In Indian mining the government is the landlord, the biggest shareholder, the price-setter for coal and the tax collector, all at once. That makes the rulebook unusually important.

Start with the landlord. The Ministry of Mines and the mining law decide who can dig for non-coal minerals and on what terms, through auctions and royalty rates. The Ministry of Coal owns Coal India, allocates and auctions coal blocks and notifies coal prices. Since 2020, commercial coal mining has been open to private companies, which slowly introduces competition to a sector that was a near-monopoly for decades.

Then the newest chapter: critical minerals. Lithium, graphite, rare earths, cobalt and the like are the raw materials of batteries, electronics and defence, and China dominates their processing. India's National Critical Mineral Mission, approved by the Cabinet in January 2025, aims to explore and auction these minerals at home, encourage companies to buy assets abroad and build up stockpiles. For listed miners and processors it is a genuine new growth avenue, though a slow one: an auctioned block today is a producing mine many years from now.

The tax collector has been busy too. In 2024 a nine-judge bench of the Supreme Court ruled that states can levy taxes on mineral rights, including back dues. That adds a state-level cost that could grow, especially in mineral-rich states looking for revenue.

And the shareholder. The government's divestment programme sells slices of Coal India, NMDC, Hindustan Zinc and others through offers for sale. Each sale is a supply event for the stock. Add the always-present environment ministry, the mine safety directorate and the power to tax ore exports, and you have a sector where reading the gazette is part of the job.
c8.read:
Each row is a regulator or rule. Read across: who it is, what it does, why you care, and its status. Then group the rows by status.

  • Always: the Ministry of Mines, the Ministry of Coal, the environment ministry, the mine safety directorate DGMS, and export duty powers. Five of eight rows are permanent fixtures, which says how embedded the state is in this industry. They rarely make headlines, but when they do, a mine shuts, a project slips or a price changes.
  • Live: the Supreme Court ruling on mineral taxes and the divestment programme. These are the two rows most likely to move a stock in the near term: a new state levy hits costs, and an offer for sale caps a share price for a few weeks.
  • New: the critical minerals mission. A slow tailwind and a source of optionality for processors and miners that win blocks or overseas assets.

Notice that there is no coming row. Unlike steel or chemicals, mining has no large external rule bearing down on it right now; its policy risk comes from inside, from Delhi and the state capitals.

A practical habit: for Coal India, NMDC and Hindustan Zinc, keep an eye out for offer-for-sale announcements, which come with little notice. For smelters, watch the export duty row whenever domestic prices spike.

Dated regulatory news for mining, filtered from our feed, sits on the Picks and signals tab.

c9.story:
Porter's five forces asks who keeps the profit: rivals, suppliers, customers, newcomers or substitutes. For the best Indian miners the honest answer is: mostly themselves.

Take Coal India. It supplies most of India's coal, so domestic rivalry is limited; the real competitor is imported coal, which is often more expensive once freight is added. Its supplies are the ground under its feet and its own workforce. New entrants exist since commercial mining opened in 2020, but a new coal mine takes years of clearances. Hindustan Zinc looks similar: it produces most of India's zinc from some of the world's richest deposits. That is why both score so low on rivalry and suppliers.

Customers are the one area where the majors give something back. Power utilities and steel mills are giant buyers, and the government stands behind the utilities. Metal buyers simply pay the London price, so there is no haggling, but there is also no premium for being Indian.

Iron ore miners and processors face a tougher picture. NMDC sells to a steel industry that is consolidating into a few powerful groups, some of which now mine their own ore. A ferro alloy maker or graphite electrode maker buys ore or electricity from others and sells into a market where Chinese producers can flood supply whenever they choose. Graphite India learned both sides of this: when China shut polluting electrode capacity in 2017 and 2018, prices went vertical and profits exploded; when Chinese supply came back, the boom deflated.

Substitutes score the same for both groups and they are slow: solar eating into coal, aluminium replacing copper in some cables and steel in some car parts.
c9.read:
The radar has five spokes, one per force. The further a shape reaches out along a spoke, the more pressure on the business, so a smaller shape is the better business.

Two shapes are drawn: coal and base-metal majors, and iron ore and processors. Look at overall size first. The majors' shape is small and lopsided: tight on rivalry and suppliers, which score just one, and on new entrants, which scores half. The processors' shape is bigger on all three: two on rivalry and suppliers, one and a half on entrants.

Now look at where the two shapes meet. On buyers both score two, because power utilities and steel mills are big, organised customers, and metal buyers pay the London price regardless of who sells. On substitutes both score one and a half: solar against coal, aluminium against copper and steel. Those shared spokes are the pressures the whole sector shares, regardless of quality.

The table beside the chart gives each score from zero to three with its reason. If a particular company does not fit its group, say a processor with its own captive power, redraw its supplier spoke in your head, and the shape shrinks accordingly.

The gap between the two shapes is the same idea as the profit bars on card one, drawn a different way. The majors, with captive ore and power, keep most of the profit at almost any price. The processors keep little and swing with the Chinese price of their one product.

c10.story:
Mining results calls are full of tonnes, grades, strip ratios and recovery rates. You can safely skip most of it. Eight numbers tell you nearly everything, and half of them are about one question: what does it cost this company to produce a tonne, compared with everyone else in the world?

Cost of production per tonne comes first. It tells you where the company sits on the global cost curve. A miner in the bottom quarter of that curve makes money even at the bottom of the cycle, which is precisely the kind of company you want to own going into a downturn. EBITDA margin tells you how much of the price the company keeps, and for the best Indian producers it is remarkably high in a good year.

Production volume is the growth question: are mines and smelters expanding without the cost per tonne creeping up? For coal, the e-auction premium over the notified price is a thermometer for how tight the market is. A fat premium means power plants and factories are scrambling for coal; a thin one means they are not.

Then the two cost lines that define the two halves of the sector. Employee cost as a share of sales is the number to watch at Coal India, where people are the biggest expense. Power and fuel as a share of sales is the number for smelters, where electricity is the biggest expense.

Finally, the balance sheet and the verdict. Net debt to EBITDA matters mainly for the Vedanta group, where it has been the defining issue for years. And return on capital employed tells you whether the whole enterprise earns its keep through a full cycle, booms and busts included.
c10.read:
One row per number. Read across: what the number tells you, what good looks like, and today's industry median.

  • What it tells you: notice that the first row, cost per tonne, is the only one about position rather than performance. It tells you how the company will fare in the next bust, not how it did last quarter.
  • What good looks like: the benchmark, and the only column with figures. Several rows specify which company type the benchmark applies to: the EBITDA margin row gives separate marks for Hindustan Zinc, aluminium and Coal India; the employee row applies to coal and the power row to smelters. Do not judge a smelter by the coal benchmark.
  • Today's industry median: from the latest filings of listed miners in our database. Cost per tonne and the e-auction premium show no median, because those come from company presentations and auction results rather than standard accounts.

One caution on medians in this sector: the listed group mixes coal, metals and small processors, so the median is an average of very different businesses. It is most useful for the EBITDA margin and ROCE rows, as a quick check on where the sector as a whole sits in the cycle; in a boom, the median margin should be well up.

The best use is a three-way comparison for each company: its own number, the median and the good mark. For a metal major, its EBITDA margin against its own boom-year margin is often the most telling comparison of all.

c11.story:
Mining is one of the few sectors where you can watch the main revenue driver move every day. London metal prices tick in real time, and for a metal major they translate into this quarter's realisation almost mechanically. So the trick in mining is not finding the signal; it is figuring out which signals tell you about the next quarter rather than this one.

The same-quarter signals are the London prices themselves, power demand and heatwaves, and the monthly coal and mineral production data. They tell you what the quarter you are in will look like before the company reports it.

The one-quarter-ahead signals are where the edge is. Chinese industrial output and credit data tell you where London prices are heading. Coal stockpiles at power plants tell you about Coal India's offtake: full stockpiles today mean weaker demand for fresh coal next quarter. The dollar index matters because metals are priced in dollars, and a weaker dollar tends to lift them. Global smelter shutdowns and mine outages, say a copper mine flooding or a European smelter closing on power costs, raise prices for everyone still running.

Put it together and you get the three-sign rule. Mining is in a full up-cycle when London metal prices are rising, Chinese demand is firming and Indian power demand is strong. Today two out of three are ticking: London prices are strong and Indian power demand is growing. The missing sign is China, still soft, with stimulus hoped for rather than delivered. That makes this a partial boom, carried by the energy-transition metals rather than by a broad Chinese recovery.

This metals boom is running on grids, cars and data centres, not on Chinese apartments. That is new, and it is the whole debate.
c11.read:
The chart places each outside signal by how far ahead it speaks. The further right a dot sits, the earlier the warning. Hover a dot to read its channel into earnings.

  • Same quarter, far left: daily London metal prices, power demand and heatwaves, and monthly production data. Three dots that tell you what is happening now.
  • One quarter ahead: Chinese industrial output and credit, coal stockpiles at power plants, the dollar index, and smelter shutdowns and mine outages. Four dots.

Notice what is missing: no dots two or three quarters out. Mining is a fast-reacting sector because its prices are set in liquid markets every day, so its warnings come late. That is a reason to check the one-quarter dots every month, not every quarter.

Below the chart sits the rule with its three signs. A tick means on, a cross means off, and the note gives today's reading. London prices rising: a tick, with copper, aluminium and silver strong. Chinese demand firming: a cross, still soft. Indian power demand strong: a tick, though the note adds that stockpiles are full, which is why coal is not benefiting. Two ticks, a partial boom.

The call box gives the direction, the three points behind it and what would change it: a Chinese slump or a dollar rally that knocks London prices down, a new export duty or state mineral tax, or a heatwave-driven coal shortage that revives e-auction premiums. The first two would hurt the metal majors; the third would wake up Coal India.
